entries.ae06e141db66996ae2e8fa16dc0d7a7d4c396664: <div eID="gen23934" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23935" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23936" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23936" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23935" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23937" type="x-p"/> A farther exhortation to acquire wisdom, in order to be preserved from impure connections, <reference osisRef="Pro.7.1-Pro.7.5">Pro 7:1-5</reference>. The character of a harlot, and her conduct towards a youth who fell into her snare, vv. 6-23. Solemn exhortations to avoid this evil, <reference osisRef="Pro.7.24-Pro.7.27">Pro 7:24-27</reference>. <div eID="gen23937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23938" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23939" type="x-p"/> My son, keep my words - See <reference osisRef="Pro.2.1">Pro 2:1</reference>.
entries.5db2e3a07648afde8341a1140e541a7658c803ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23940" type="x-p"/> As the apple of thine eye - As the pupil of the eye, which is of such essential necessity to sight, and so easily injured.
entries.43e608b5f5110a2d44206774f5db7c2642fed9fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23941" type="x-p"/> Bind them upon thy fingers - See on <reference osisRef="Pro.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference> (note).
entries.3bd5c94009d7af27a910dc887a8624508386c892: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23942" type="x-p"/> Thou art my sister - Thou art my dearest friend, and I will treat thee as such.
entries.e28987f3fa48d5ceed168a4ee01567eb3850c3a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23943" type="x-p"/> The strange woman - The prostitute, the adulteress.
entries.356d24407edd6e7f7cc26738095b43641fe6b00b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23944" type="x-p"/> I looked through my casement - The casement is a small aperture in a large window, or a window opening on hinges. Here it means the lattice, for they had no glass windows in the East. And the latticed windows produced a double advantage <div eID="gen23944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23945" type="x-p"/> 1. Making the apartments sufficiently private; and <div eID="gen23945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23946" type="x-p"/> 2. Admitting fresh air to keep them cool.
entries.95232d004e9b38b44fc426b4ca4f9b448d1825fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23947" type="x-p"/> Among the simple ones - The inexperienced, inconsiderate young men. <div eID="gen23947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23948" type="x-p"/> A young man void of understanding - בעל ראשאהץ חסר לב, "destitute of a heart." He had not wisdom to discern the evil intended; nor courage to resist the flatteries of the seducer.
entries.172fe972c1569a1a66538b46074e485c91195035: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23949" type="x-p"/> He went the way to her house - She appears to have had a corner house sufficiently remarkable; and a way from the main street to it.
entries.b08e3ce2351751b143375d9cf19cbfe148ab2148: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23950" type="x-p"/> In the twilight, in the evening - Some time after sun-setting; before it was quite dark. <div eID="gen23950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23951" type="x-p"/> In the black and dark night - When there were neither lamps nor moon-shine.
entries.595b489ecd705219a01cf0938db892bd535f5146: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23952" type="x-p"/> A woman with the attire of a harlot - It appears that sitting in some open place, and covering the face, or having a veil of a peculiar kind on, was the evidence of a harlot, <reference osisRef="Gen.38.14">Gen 38:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.38.15-Gen.38.19">Gen 38:15-19</reference>. No doubt, in Solomon's time, they had other distinctions. In all other countries, and in all times. the show of their countenance did testify against them; they declared their sin as Sodom; they hid it not. However, this does not seem to have been a mere prostitute; for she was, according to her own declaration, a married woman, and kept house, <reference osisRef="Pro.7.19">Pro 7:19</reference>, if her assertions relative to this were not falsehoods, and calculated the better to render him secure, and prevent the suspicion of endangering himself by cohabiting with a common woman; which I am rather inclined to think was the case, for she was subtle of heart.
entries.2cd023e5000aa8aacb280beeb35cb709e61cd377: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23953" type="x-p"/> She is loud and stubborn - המיה homiyah, she is never at rest, always agitated; busily employed to gain her end, and this is to go into the path of error: סררת sorereth, "turning aside;" preferring any way to the right way. And, therefore, it is added, her feet abide not in her house, she gads abroad; and this disposition probably first led her to this vice.
entries.cbb599dd79371fee3992abca771df2a5f0a27737: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23954" type="x-p"/> Now is she without - She is continually exposing herself, and showing by her gait and gestures what she is, and what she wants. These two verses are a parenthesis, intended to show the character of the woman.
entries.76ebda6944654cc996c87d9606f6a07cde90720f: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23955" type="x-p"/> So she caught him - Laid fast hold on him, and kissed him, to show that she was affectionately attached to him. <div eID="gen23955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23956" type="x-p"/> And with an impudent face - העזה פניה heezzah paneyha, "she strengthened her countenance," assumed the most confident look she could; endeavored to appear friendly and sincere.
entries.f020ecb63daf9a4c9e2ff7eaa29553bc81775418: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23957" type="x-p"/> I have peace-offerings with me - More literally, "the sacrifices of the peace-offerings are with me." Peace-offerings Mymlv shelamim, were offerings the spiritual design of which was to make peace between God and man, to make up the breach between them which sin had occasioned; see the notes on Leviticus 7 (note), where every kind of sacrifice offered under the law is explained. When the blood of these was poured out at the altar, and the fat burnt there, the breast and right shoulder were the priest's portion; but the rest of the carcass belonged to the sacrificer, who might carry it home, and make a feast to his friends. See <reference osisRef="Lev.3.1-Lev.3.11">Lev 3:1-11</reference>. Much light is cast on this place by the fact that the gods in many parts of the East are actually worshipped in brothels, and fragments of the offerings are divided among the wretches who fall into the snare of the prostitutes - Ward's Customs. <div eID="gen23957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23958" type="x-p"/> Have I payed my vows - She seems to insinuate that she had made a vow for the health and safety of this young man; and having done so, and prepared the sacrificial banquet, came actually out to seek him, that he might partake of it with her, <reference osisRef="Pro.7.15">Pro 7:15</reference>. But, as she intended to proceed farther than mere friendship, she was obliged to avail herself of the night season, and the absence of her husband.
entries.2ab53efc2feed991ebd3238e00d7c820379e0874: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23959" type="x-p"/> I have decked my bed - ערשי arsi, "my couch or sofa;" distinguished from משכבי mishcabi, "my bed," <reference osisRef="Pro.7.17">Pro 7:17</reference>, the place to sleep on, as the other was the place to recline on at meals. The tapestry, מרבדים marbaddim, mentioned here seems to refer to the covering of the sofa; exquisitely woven and figured cloth. חטבות אטון chatuboth etun, the Targum translates painted carpets, such as were manufactured in Egypt; some kind of embroidered or embossed stuff is apparently meant.
entries.d942fc5f627ae16ee17dc38e73ac27b33ff1cff1: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23960" type="x-p"/> I have perfumed any bed with Myrrh - מר mor, "aloes," אהלים ahalim, and "cinnamon," קנמון kinnamon. We have taken our names from the original words; but probably the ahalim may not mean aloes, which is no perfume; but sandal wood, which is very much used in the East. She had used every means to excite the passions she wished to bring into action.
entries.e444bd6ae9fefb05791ceb0ee9106673109ad4a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23961" type="x-p"/> Come, let us take our fill of love - נרוה דדים nirveh dodim, "Let us revel in the breasts;" and then it is added, "Let us solace ourselves with loves," נתעלסה באהבים nithallesah boohabim; "let us gratify each other with loves, with the utmost delights." This does not half express the original; but I forbear. The speech shows the brazen face of this woman, well translated by the Vulgate, "Veni, inebriemur uberibus; et fruamur cupidinis amplexibus." And the Septuagint has expressed the spirit of it: Ελθε, και απολαυσωμεν φιλιας - δευρο, και εγκυλισθωμεν ερωτι. "Veni, et fruamur amicitia - Veni, et colluctemur cupidine." Though varied in the words, all the versions have expressed the same thing. In the old MS. Bible, the speech of this woman is as follows: I have arrayed with cordis my litil bed, and spred with peyntid tapetis of Egipt: I have springid my ligginge place with mirre and aloes and calelcum, and be we inwardly drunken with Tetis, and use we the coveytied clippingis to the tyme that the dai wax light. The original itself is too gross to be literally translated; but quite in character as coming from the mouth of an abandoned woman.
entries.652be4e00b58109dc7b630d53f7ebd3f9ff37f51: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen23961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23962" type="x-p"/> For the good man - Literally, "For the man is not in his house."
entries.dd9f8bbcb7ddb4526beaac9b9f46079bf2e8c0a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen23962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23963" type="x-p"/> He hath taken - Literally, "The money bag he hath taken in his hand." He is gone a journey of itinerant merchandising. This seems to be what is intended. <div eID="gen23963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23964" type="x-p"/> And will come home at the day appointed - ליום הכסא leyom hakkase, the time fixed for a return from such a journey. The Vulgate says, "at the full moon." The Targum, "the day of the assembly." In other words, He will return by the approaching festival.
entries.fd5ba2c8dc544f77d8dfe3e7631d03b7fa576e04: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen23964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23965" type="x-p"/> With her much fair speech - With her blandishments and lascivious talk, she overcame all his scruples, and constrained him to yield.
entries.60b823640fec7f3e14f45e4dc97c08d9c3997e93: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen23965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23966" type="x-p"/> As an ox goeth to the slaughter - The original of this and the following verse has been variously translated. Dr. Grey corrects and translates thus: "He goeth after her straightway, as an Ox goeth to the Slaughter; as a Dog to the Chain; and as a Deer till the Dart strike through his liver; as a Bird hasteneth to the Snare, and knoweth not that it is for its life." Very slight alterations in the Hebrew text produce these differences; but it is not necessary to pursue them; all serve to mark the stupidity and folly of the man who is led away by enticing women or who lives a life of intemperance.
entries.885010c4a419f58d12ca90ece8dcbf5b5621791c: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen23966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23967" type="x-p"/> Hearken unto me now, therefore, O ye children - Ye that are young and inexperienced, seriously consider the example set before your eyes, and take warning at another's expense.
entries.dcf07acf5b1f746f5dd222e2698071b208436fcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen23967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23968" type="x-p"/> For she hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong men have been slain by her - That is, such like women have been the ruin of many. חללים chalalim, which we render wounded, also signifies solsliers or men of war; and עצמים atsumim, which we render strong men, may be translated heroes. Many of those who have distinguished themselves in the field and in the cabinet have been overcome and destroyed by their mistresses. History is full of such examples.
entries.435dfd231b5e0f3b5d6c5a17158f909d39dd9a1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen23968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23969" type="x-p"/> Her house is the way to hell - שאול sheol, the pit, the grave, the place of the dead, the eternal and infernal world. And they who, through such, fall into the grave, descend lower, into the chambers of death; the place where pleasure is at an end, and illusion mocks no more.  <chapter eID="Prov.7"/> <div eID="gen23969" type="x-p"/>

entries.a1ad9838bb92997e91b123ff1f2ed8a2cf47a675: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.1-Prov.7.3">Pro 7:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen10762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10763" type="x-p"/> The introduction first counsels in general to a true appreciation of these well-considered life-rules of wisdom. 1 My son, keep my words,    And treasure up my commandments with thee. 2 Keep my commandments, and thou shalt live;    And my instruction as the apple of thine eye. 3 Wind them about thy fingers,    Write them on the tablet of thy heart. <div eID="gen10763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10764" type="x-p"/> The lxx has after <reference osisRef="Prov.7.1">Pro 7:1</reference> another distich; but it here disturbs the connection. Regarding צפן, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.1">Pro 2:1</reference>; אתּך refers, as there, to the sphere of one’s own character, and that subjectively. Regarding the <hi type="italic">imper</hi>. וחיה, which must here be translated according to its sense as a conclusion, because it comes in between the objects governed by שׁמר, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 4:4. There וחיה is punctuated with <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>; here, according to Kimchi (<hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 125a), with <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>-<hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, וחיה, as in the Cod. Erfurt. 2 and 3, and in the editions of Athias and Clodius, so that the word belongs to the class פתחין באתנח (with short instead of long vowel by the pausal accent): no reason for this is to be perceived, especially as (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.4">Pro 4:4</reference>) the <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi> (ê from aj) which is characteristic of the imper. remains unchanged. Regarding אישׁון העין, Arab. insân el-'ain, the little man of the eye, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the apple of the eye, named from the miniature portrait of him who looks into it being reflected from it, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; the ending ôn is here diminutive, like Syr. achuno, little brother, beruno, little son, and the like. On <reference osisRef="Prov.7.3">Pro 7:3</reference>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.6.21">Pro 6:21</reference>; Pro 3:3. The תפילין שׁל יד<note placement="foot">תפילין, prayer-fillets, phylacteries.</note> were wound seven times round the left arm and seven times round the middle finger. The writing on the table of the heart may be regarded as referring to <reference osisRef="Deut.6.9">Deu 6:9</reference> (the Mezuzoth).<note placement="foot">= the door-posts, afterwards used by the Jews to denote the passages of Scripture written on the door-posts.</note>
entries.180f5750c54bee4449e47076136ae22b09345760: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.4-Prov.7.5">Pro 7:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen10764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> The subject-matter of this earnest warning are the admonitions of the teacher of wisdom, and through him of Wisdom herself, who in contrast to the world and its lust is the worthiest object of love, and deserves to be loved with the purest, sincerest love: 4 Say to wisdom: “Thou art my sister!”    And call understanding “Friend;” 5 That they may keep thee from the strange woman,    From the stranger who useth smooth words. <div eID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> The childlike, sisterly, and friendly relationship serves also to picture forth and designate the intimate confidential relationship to natures and things which are not flesh and blood. If in Arabic the poor is called the brother of poverty, the trustworthy the brother of trustworthiness, and abu, um (אם), achu, ucht, are used in manifold ways as the expression for the interchangeable relation between two ideas; so (as also, notwithstanding Ewald, §273b, in many Hebr. proper names) that has there become national, which here, as at <reference osisRef="Job.17.14">Job 17:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.29">Job 30:29</reference>, mediated by the connection of the thoughts, only first appears as a poetic venture. The figurative words of <reference osisRef="Prov.7.4">Pro 7:4</reference> not merely lead us to think of wisdom as a personal existence of a higher order, but by this representation it is itself brought so near, that אם easily substitutes itself, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.3">Pro 2:3</reference>, in the place of אם. אחתי of Solomon’s address to the bride brought home is in its connection compared with Book of Wisdom 8:2. While the ôth of אחות by no means arises from abstr. ûth, but achôth is derived from achajath, מודע (as Rth 2:1, cf. מודעת, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.2">Pro 3:2</reference>), here by <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> מודע, properly means acquaintance, and then the person known, but not in the superficial sense in which this word and the Arab. ma'arfat are used (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in the Arabic phrase quoted by Fleischer, kanna aṣḥaab ṣarna m'aaraf - <hi type="italic">nous étions amis, nous en sommes plus que de simples connaissances</hi>), but in the sense of familiar, confidential alliance. The <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. לשׁמרך does not need for its explanation some intermediate thought to be introduced: <hi type="italic">quod eo conducet tibi ut</hi> (Mich.), but connects itself immediately as the purpose: bind wisdom to thyself and thyself to wisdom thus closely that thou mayest therewith guard thyself. As for the rest, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pro 2:16</reference>; this verse repeats itself here with the variation of one word.
entries.2f4a97c195d19dea0b745bb3c0a19c82e8db7826: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.6-Prov.7.7">Pro 7:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> How necessary it is for the youth to guard himself by the help of wisdom against the enticements of the wanton woman, the author now shows by a reference to his own observation. 6 For through the window of my house,    From behind the lattice I looked out; 7 Then saw I among the simple ones,    Discerned among the young people, a youth devoid of understanding. כּי refers indeed to the immediately following clause, yet it actually opens up the whole following exemplification. The connection with <reference osisRef="Prov.7.5">Pro 7:5</reference> would be closer if instead of the extended Semitic construction it were said: <hi type="italic">nam quum ...prospicerem vidi</hi>, etc. חלּון (from חלל, to bore through) is properly a place where the wall is bored through. אשׁנב .hguor (from שׁנב = Arab. shaniba, to be agreeable, cool, fresh) is the window-lattice or lattice-window, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, lattice for drawing down and raising up, which keeps off the rays of the sun. נשׁקף signifies primarily to make oneself long in order to see, to stretch up or out the neck and the head, καραδοκεῖν, Arab. atall, atal'a, and tatall'a of things, <hi type="italic">imminere</hi>, to overtop, to project, to jut in; cf. Arab. askaf of the ostrich, long and bent, with respect to the neck stretching it up, sakaf, <hi type="italic">abstr</hi>. crooked length. And בּעד is thus used, as in Arab. duna, but not b'ad, is used: so placed, that one in relation to the other obstructs the avenue to another person or thing: “I looked forth from behind the lattice-window, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, with respect to the persons or things in the room, standing before the lattice-window, and thus looking out into the open air” (Fleischer). That it was far in the night, as we learn at <reference osisRef="Prov.7.9">Pro 7:9</reference>, does not contradict this looking out; for apart from the moon, and especially the lighting of the streets, there were star-lit nights, and to see what the narrator saw there was no night of Egyptian darkness. But because it was night 6a is not to be translated: I looked about among those devoid of experience (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Löwenstein); but he saw among these, observed among the youths, who thus late amused themselves without, a young man whose want of understanding was manifest from what further happened. Bertheau: that I might see, is syntactically impossible. The meaning of וארא is not determined by the אבינה following, but conversely אבינה stands under the operation of ו (= אבינה, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.7">Neh 13:7</reference>), characterizing the historic aorist. Regarding פּתי, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 1:4. בּנים is the masc. of בּנות, Arab. benât in the meaning maiden. בבּנים has in correct texts, according to the rules of the accents, the ב <hi type="italic">raphatum</hi>.<note placement="foot">Regarding the Targ. of <reference osisRef="Prov.7.6-Prov.7.7">Pro 7:6-7</reference>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Perles, <hi type="italic">Etymologische Studien</hi>, 1871, p. 9.</note>
entries.5ed479bda7b2304742948deb40739ead9d443abe: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.8-Prov.7.9">Pro 7:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> Now follows, whither he saw the young fop [<hi type="italic">Laffen</hi>] then go in the darkness. 8 Going up and down the street near her corner,    And he walked along the way to her house, 9 In the twilight, when the day declined,    In the midst of the night and deep darkness. <div eID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10769" type="x-p"/> We may interpret עבר as appos.: <hi type="italic">juvenem amentem, ambulantem</hi>, or as the predicate accus.: <hi type="italic">vidi juvenem ... ambulantem</hi>; for that one may so express himself in Hebrew (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.7">Dan 8:7</reference>), Hitzig unwarrantably denies. The passing over of the part. into the finite, 8b, is like <reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">Pro 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pro 2:17</reference>, and that of the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.27">Pro 1:27</reference>; Pro 2:8. שׁוּק, Arab. suk (dimin. suweiḳa, to separate, from sikkat, street, alley), still means, as in former times, a broad street, a principal street, as well as an open place, a market-place where business is transacted, or according to its etymon: where cattle are driven for sale. On the street he went backwards and forwards, yet so that he kept near to her corner (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of the woman whom he waited for), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he never withdrew himself far from the corner of her house, and always again returned to it. The corner is named, because from that place he could always cast a look over the front of the house to see whether she whom he waited for showed herself. Regarding פּנּהּ for פּנּתהּ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference> : a primary form פּן has never been in use; פּנּים, Zec 14:10, is plur. of פּנּהּ. אצל (from אצל, Arab. wasl, to bind) is, as a substantive, the side (as the place where one thing connects itself with another), and thus as a preposition it means (like <hi type="italic">juxta</hi> from <hi type="italic">jungere</hi>) beside, Ital. <hi type="italic">allato</hi>. דּרכו is the object. accus., for thus are construed verbs <hi type="italic">eundi</hi> (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.12">Hab 3:12</reference>, Num. 30:17, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">Pro 21:22</reference>).
entries.ea0f0e03bcd672ee17f5dd91d5a56c3358b00c9a: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.10-Prov.7.12">Pro 7:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen10770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10771" type="x-p"/> Finally, the young man devoid of understanding sees his waiting rewarded: like meets like. 10 And, lo, a woman coming to meet him,      In the attire of an harlot and of subtle heart. 11 Boisterous is she, and ungovernable;      Her feet have no rest in her own house. 12 At one time before her door, at another in the street,      And again at every corner she places herself on the watch. “Pro 7:12 (Hitzig) expresses what is wont to be, instead of a single event, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference>, viz., the custom of a street harlot. But she who is spoken of is not such an one; lurking is not applicable to her (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.31.9">Job 31:9</reference>), and, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference>, it is not meant that she is thus inclined.” But Hitzig’s rendering of <reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference>, “she was boisterous ... in her house her feet had no rest,” is inaccurate, since neither היאו nor שׁכנוּ is used. Thus in <reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.7.12">Pro 7:12</reference> the poet gives a characteristic of the woman, introduced by הנּהו into the frame of his picture, which goes beyond that which then presented itself to his eyes. We must with <reference osisRef="Prov.7.12">Pro 7:12</reference> reject also <reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference>; and even that would not be a radical improvement, since that characteristic lying behind the evident, that which was then evident begins with וּנצרת לב (and subtle in heart). We must thus suppose that the woman was not unknown to the observer here describing her. He describes her first as she then appeared. שׁית Hitzig regards as equivalent to שׁוית, similitude (from שׁוה), and why? Because שׁית does not mean “to lay against,” but “to place.” But <reference osisRef="Exod.33.4">Exo 33:4</reference> shows the contrary, and justifies the meaning attire, which the word also has in Psa 73:6. <hi type="italic">Meîri</hi> less suitably compares 2Ki 9:30, but rightly explains תקון (dressing, ornament), and remarks that שׁית elliptical is equivalent to בּשׁית. It is not the nominative (Bertheau), but the accusative, as תבנית, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12">Psa 144:12</reference>, Ewald, §279d. How Hitzig reaches the translation of ונצרת לב by “and an arrow in her heart” (<hi type="italic">et saucia corde</hi>)<note placement="foot">Virgil’s <hi type="italic">Aeneid</hi>, iv. 1.</note> one can only understand by reading his commentary. The usage of the language, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.23">Pro 4:23</reference>, he remarks, among other things, would stamp her as a virtuous person. As if a phrase like נצר לב could be used both <hi type="italic">sensu bono</hi> and <hi type="italic">sensu malo</hi>! One can guard his heart when he protects it carefully against moral danger, or also when he purposely conceals that which is in it. The <hi type="italic">part</hi>. נצוּר signifies, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Isa 1:8</reference>, besieged (blockaded), <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.12">Eze 16:12</reference>, protected, guarded, and <reference osisRef="Isa.48.6">Isa 48:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">Isa 65:4</reference>, concealed, hidden. Ewald, §187b, refers these three significations in the two passages in Isaiah and in the passage before us to צרר, <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נצר (as נגל); but (1) one would then more surely take צוּר (cf. נמּול, נבכים) as the verbal stem; (2) one reaches the idea of the concealed (the hidden) easier from that of the preserved than from that of the confined. As one says in Lat. <hi type="italic">homo occultus, tectus, abstrusus</hi>, in the sense of κρυψίνους, so it is said of that woman נצרת לב, not so much in the sense of <hi type="italic">retenta cor, h.e. quae quod in corde haberet non pandebat</hi>, Fr. <hi type="italic">retenue</hi> (Cocc.), as in the sense of <hi type="italic">custodita cor, quae intentionem cordis mentemque suam callide novit premere</hi> (Mich.): she is of a hidden mind, of a concealed nature; for she feigns fidelity to her husband and flatters her paramours as her only beloved, while in truth she loves none, and each of them is to her only a means to an end, viz., to the indulgence of her worldly sensual desire. For, as the author further describes here, she is המיּה (fem. of המה = המי, as <reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Pro 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference>), <hi type="italic">tumultuosa</hi>, externally as internally impetuous, because full of intermingling lust and deceit (<hi type="italic">opp</hi>. ἡσύχιος, 1Pe 3:4; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>), and סררת, self-willed, not minding the law of duty, of discretion, or of modesty (from סרר, Arab. sharr, <hi type="italic">pervicacem, malum esse</hi>). She is the very opposite of the noiseless activity and the gentle modesty of a true house-wife, rude, stubborn, and also vagrant like a beast in its season (Hos 4:14): <hi type="italic">in domo ipsius residere nequeunt pedes ejus</hi>; thus not οἰκουρός or οἰκουργός (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.5">Tit 2:5</reference>), far removed from the genuine woman - like εἴσω ἥσυχον μένειν δόμων<note placement="foot">Eurip. <hi type="italic">Herac</hi>.) - a radt, as they call such a one in Arab. (Wünsche on Hos 12:1</note> or as she is called in Aram. נפקת בּרא.
entries.34604841052c71f73c7a91466a91659a86d0b23a: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">Pro 7:13</reference> <div eID="gen10772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> After this digression the poet returns to the subject, and further describes the event as observed by himself. <div eID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> And she laid hold on him and kissed him; <div eID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> Put on a bold brow and said to him. <div eID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> The verb נשׁק is here, after its primary signification, connected with the dat.: <hi type="italic">osculum fixit ei</hi>. Thus also <reference osisRef="Gen.27.26">Gen 27:26</reference> is construed, and the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in לּו is, as there, <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conj</hi>., after the law for which the national grammarians have coined the technical name אתי מרחיק (<hi type="italic">veniens e longinquo</hi>, “coming out of the distance,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the attraction of a word following by one accented on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>.). The <hi type="italic">penult</hi>.-accenting of נשׁקה is the consequence of the retrogression of the accent (נסוג אחור), which, here where the word from the first had the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>, only with <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, and thus with a half a tone, brings with it the dageshing of the לו following, as the original penultima-accenting of והחזיקה does of the בו which follows it, for the reading בּו by Löwenstein is contrary to the laws of punctuation of the <hi type="italic">Textus receptus</hi> under consideration here.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 29f., and <hi type="italic">Psalmen-Commentar</hi> under Psa 52:5.</note> <div eID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> As בו and לו have received the doubling <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, so on the other hand, according to Ewald, §193b, it has disappeared from העזה (written with <hi type="italic">Raphe</hi> according to Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 145a). And as נשׁקה has the tone thrown back, so the proper pausal ותּאמר is accented on the ult., but without attracting the לו following by dageshing, which is the case only when the first of the two words terminates in the sound of ā (āh). העז פניו is said of one who shows firmness of hardness of countenance (Arab. slabt alwajh), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, one who shows shamelessness, or, as we say, an iron forehead (Fl.).
entries.e188eaada31053ca2e123ce3604e9bc705f1417a: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14-Prov.7.15">Pro 7:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> She laid hold on him and kissed him, both of which actions were shameless, and then, assuming the passivity and modesty befitting the woman, and disregarding morality and the law, she said to the youth: 14 “To bring peace-offerings was binding upon me,      To-day have I redeemed my vows. 15 Therefore am I come out to meet thee,      To seek thy face, and have found thee.” <div eID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10779" type="x-p"/> We have translated זבחי שׁלמים “peace-offerings,” proceeding on the principle that שׁלם (sing. only <reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">Amo 5:22</reference>, and on the Phoenician altar at Marseilles) denotes contracting friendship with one (from שׁלם, to hold friendly relationship), and then the gifts having this in view; for the idea of this kind of offering is the attestation and confirmation of communion with God. But in view of the derivatives שׁלמנים and שׁלּוּם, it is perhaps more appropriate to combine שׁלם with שׁלּם, to discharge perfectly, and to translate it thank-payment-offering, or with v. Hofmann, a due-offering, where not directly thank-offering; for the proper eucharistic offering, which is the expression of thanks on a particular occasion, is removed from the species of the <hi type="italic">Shelamim</hi> by the addition of the words על־תּודה (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.12-Lev.7.25">Lev 7:12-25</reference>). The characteristic of the <hi type="italic">Shelamim</hi> is the division of the flesh of the sacrifice between Jahve and His priests on the one side, and the person (or persons) bringing it on the other side: only one part of the flesh of the sacrifice was Jahve’s, consumed by fire (<reference osisRef="Lev.3.16">Lev 3:16</reference>); the priests received one part; those who brought the offering received back another part as it were from the altar of God, that they might eat it with holy joy along with their household. So here the adulteress says that there was binding upon her, in consequence of a vow she had taken, the duty of presenting peace-offerings, or offerings that were due; to-day (she reckons the day in the sense of the <hi type="italic">dies civilis</hi> from night to night) she has performed her duties, and the שׁלמי נדר have yielded much to her that she might therewith regale him, her true lover; for with על־כּן she means to say that even the prospect of the gay festival which she can prepare for him moved her thus to meet him. This address of the woman affords us a glimpse into the history of the customs of those times. The <hi type="italic">Shelamim</hi> meals degenerated in the same manner as our <hi type="italic">Kirmsen</hi>.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Kirmse</hi> = anniversary of the dedication of a church, village fête.</note> <div eID="gen10779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> Secularization lies doubly near to merrymaking when the law sanctions this, and it can conceal itself behind the mask of piety. Regarding שׁחר, a more exact word for בּקּשׁ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 1:28. To seek the countenance of one is equivalent to to seek his person, himself, but yet not without reference to the wished-for look [<hi type="italic">aspectus</hi>] of the person.
entries.cc566649fe8f636640ff665d6e5dad1db96e680e: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.16-Prov.7.18">Pro 7:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10781" type="x-p"/> Thus she found him, and described to him the enjoyment which awaited him in eating and drinking, then in the pleasures of love. 16 “My bed have I spread with cushions,      Variegated coverlets, Egyptian linen; 17 I have sprinkled my couch      With myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. 18 Come then, we will intoxicate ourselves with love till the morning,      And will satisfy ourselves in love.” <div eID="gen10781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10782" type="x-p"/> The noun ערשׂ, from ערשׂ, = Arab. 'arash, <hi type="italic">aedificare, fabricari</hi>, signifies generally the wooden frame; thus not so much the bed within as the erected bed-place (cf. Arab. 'arsh, throne, and 'arysh, arbour). This bedstead she had richly and beautifully cushioned, that it might be soft and agreeable. רבד, from רב, signifies to lay on or apply closely, thus either <hi type="italic">vincire</hi> (whence the name of the necklace, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.42">Gen 41:42</reference>) or <hi type="italic">sternere</hi> (different from רפד, <reference osisRef="Job.17.13">Job 17:13</reference>, which acquires the meaning <hi type="italic">sternere</hi> from the root-meaning to raise up from under, <hi type="italic">sublevare</hi>), whence מרבדּים, cushions, pillows, <hi type="italic">stragulae</hi>. Böttcher punctuates מרבדּים incorrectly; the ב remains aspirated, and the connection of the syllables is looser than in מרבּה, Ewald, §88d. The צטבות beginning the second half-verse is in no case an adjective to מרבדים, in every case only appos., probably an independent conception; not derived from חטב (cogn. חצב), to hew wood (whence Arab. ḥaṭab, fire-wood), according to which Kimchi, and with him the <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> (περιξύστοις), understands it of the carefully polished bed-poles or bed-boards, but from חטב = Arab. khaṭeba, to be streaked, of diverse colours (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12">Psa 144:12</reference>), whence the Syriac machṭabto, a figured (striped, checkered) garment. Hitzig finds the idea of coloured or variegated here unsuitable, but without justice; for the pleasantness of a bed is augmented not only by its softness, but also by the impression which its costliness makes on the eye. The following אטוּן מצרים stands in an appositional relation to חטבות, as when one says in Arabic taub-un dı̂bâg'-un, a garment brocade = of brocade. אטוּן (after the Syr. for אטוּן, as אמוּן) signifies in the Targum the cord (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jer 38:6</reference>), like the Arab. ṭunub, Syr. (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.2">Isa 54:2</reference>) tûnob; the root is טן, not in the sense of to bind, to wind (Deitr.), but in the sense of to stretch; the thread or cord is named from the extension in regard to length, and אטון is thus thread-work, whether in weaving or spinning.<note placement="foot">Hence perhaps the Greek ὀθόνη, which Fick in his <hi type="italic">Vergl. Wörterbuch</hi> connects with the Arab. verb-root vadh, to bind, wind, clothe, but not without making thereto interrogation marks.</note> <div eID="gen10782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10783" type="x-p"/> The fame of Egyptian manufactures is still expressed in the Spanish <hi type="italic">aclabtea</hi>, fine linen cloth, which is equivalent to the modern Arabic el-ḳobṭı̂je (ḳibṭije); they had there particularly also an intimate acquaintance with the dye stuffs found in the plants and fossils of the country (Klemm’s <hi type="italic">Culturgeschichte</hi>, v. 308-310).
entries.bde3fde563fa7ed8eef691859282ac7638c31be6: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.19-Prov.7.20">Pro 7:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen10784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> The adulteress now deprives the youth of all fear; the circumstances under which her invitation is given are as favourable as possible. 19 “For the man is not at home,      He has gone on a long journey. 20 He has taken the purse with him:      He will not return home till the day of the full moon.” <div eID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10786" type="x-p"/> It is true that the article stands in האישׁ, Arab. alm'ar-fat, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, serves to define the word: the man, to whom here κατ ̓  ̓ξοχήν and alone reference can be made, viz., the husband of the adulteress (Fl.); but on the other side it is characteristic that she does not say אישׁי (as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">Gen 29:32</reference>), but ignores the relation of love and duty in which she is placed to him, and speaks of him as one standing at a distance from her (Aben-Ezra). Erroneously Vogel reads בּבּית after the Targ. instead of בּביתו. We say in Hebr. אינו בביתו, <hi type="italic">il n'est pas chez soi</hi>, as we say לקח בּידו, <hi type="italic">il a pris avec soi</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.38.10">Jer 38:10</reference>). מרחוק Hitzig seeks to connect with the verb, which, after <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Isa 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.3">Isa 22:3</reference>, is possible; for the Hebr. מרחוק (ממּרחק), far off, has frequently the meaning from afar, for the measure of length is determined not from the point of departure outward, but from the end, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Homer, <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. ii. 456; ἕκαθεν δέ τε φαίνεται αὐγή, from afar the gleam is seen, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, shines hither from the distance. Similarly we say in French, <hi type="italic">il vient du coté du nord</hi>, he comes from the north, as well as <hi type="italic">il va du coté du nord</hi>, he goes northwards. But as we do not say: he has gone on a journey far off, but: on a distant journey, so here מרחוק is virtually an adj. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Isa 5:26</reference>) equivalent to רחוקה (Num 9:10): a journey which is distant = such as from it he has a long way back. Michaelis has well remarked here: <hi type="italic">ut timorem ei penitus adimat, veluti per gradus incedit</hi>. He has undertaken a journey to a remote point, but yet more: he has taken money with him, has thus business to detain him; and still further: he has even determined the distant time of his return. צרור־הכּסף .nruter (thus to be written after Ben-Asher, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 41) is the purse (from צרר, to bind together), not one of many, but that which is his own. The terminus precedes 20b to emphasize the lateness; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on כּסא under Psa 81:4. <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ καιροῦ, after Kimchi and others, who derive כסא (כסה) from the root כס, to reckon, and regard it as denoting only a definite time. But the two passages require a special idea; and the Syr. ḳêso, which in 1Ki 12:32; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.10">2Ch 7:10</reference>, designates the time from the 15th day of the month, shows that the word denotes not, according to the Talmud, the new moon (or the new year’s day), when the moon’s disk begins to cover itself, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to fill (יתכסה), but the full moon, when it is covered, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, filled; so that thus the time of the night-scene here described is not that of the last quarter of the moon (Ewald), in which it rises at midnight, but that of the new moon (Hitzig), when the night is without moonlight. Since the derivation of the word from כסא (כסה), to cover, gives the satisfactory idea of the covering or filling of the moon’s disk, we do not seek after any other; Dietrich fixes on the root-idea of roundness, and Hitzig of vision (כסא = סכה, שׂכה, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the contrary, under <reference osisRef="Ps.143.9">Psa 143:9</reference>). The ל is that of time at which, in which, about which, anything is done; it is more indefinite than בּ would be. He will not return for some fourteen days.
entries.fed1aa54da3ba70e6189ae61f6debd3e764fa984: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.21">Pro 7:21</reference> <div eID="gen10786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10787" type="x-p"/> The result: - 21 She beguiled him by the fulness of her talking,      By the smoothness of her lips she drew him away. <div eID="gen10787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> Here is a climax. First she brought him to yield, overcoming the resistance of his mind to the last point (cf. 1Ki 11:3); then drove him, or, as we say, hurried him wholly away, viz., from the right path or conduct (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">Deu 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.11">Deu 13:11</reference>). With הטּתּוּ (= הטּתהוּ) as the chief <hi type="italic">factum</hi>, the past imperf. is interchanged, 21b. Regarding לקח, see above, p. 56. Here is the rhetoric of sin (Zöckler); and perhaps the לקח of 20a has suggested this antiphrastic לקח to the author (Hitzig), as חלק (the inverted לקח, formed like שׁפל, which is the <hi type="italic">abstr</hi>. of שׁפל as that is of חלק) and תּדּיחנּוּ are reciprocally conditioned, for the idea of the slippery (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.18">Psa 73:18</reference>) connects itself with חלק.
entries.0918e7bc5c403407cc2cdd0464ce79b8280840ba: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.22-Prov.7.23">Pro 7:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> What followed: - 22 So he goes after her at once      As an ox which goeth to the slaughter-house,      And as one bereft of reason to the restraint of fetters, 23 As a bird hastens to the net,      Without knowing that his life is at stake -      Till the arrow pierces his liver. <div eID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10790" type="x-p"/> The part. הולך (thus to be accentuated according to the rule in Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 25, with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> to the tone-syllable and <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> to the preceding open syllable) preserves the idea of the fool’s going after her. פּתאם (suddenly) fixes the point, when he all at once resolves to betake himself to the rendezvous in the house of the adulteress, now a κεπφωθείς, as the lxx translates, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as we say, a simpleton who has gone on the lime-twig. He follows her as an ox goes to the slaughter-house, unconscious that he is going thither to be slaughtered; the lxx ungrammatically destroying the attributive clause: ὥσπερ δὲ βοῦς ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἄγεται. The difficulties in וּכעכס (thus punctuated, after Kimchi, with a double <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>, and not וכעכס, as is frequently the case) multiply, and it is not to be reconciled with the traditional text. The ox appears to require another beast as a side-piece; and accordingly the lxx, Syr., and Targ. find in עכס a dog (to which from אויל they also pick out איּל, a stag), Jerome a lamb (<hi type="italic">et quasi agnus</hi> כבשׂ), Rashi a venomous serpent (perhaps after ἔχις?), Löwenstein and Malbim a rattlesnake (נחשׁ מצלצל after עכּס); but all this is mere conjecture. Symmachus’ σκιρτῶν (ἐπὶ δεσμῶν ἄφρων) is without support, and, like the favourite rendering of Schelling, <hi type="italic">et sicut saliens in vinculum cervus</hi> (איל), is unsuitable on account of the unsemitic position of the words. The noun עכס, plur. עכסים, signifies, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.18">Isa 3:18</reference>, an anklet as a female ornament (whence <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa 3:16</reference> the denom. עכּס, to make a tinkling of the anklets). In itself the word only means the fetter, <hi type="italic">compes</hi>, from עכס, Arab. 'akas, 'akash, <hi type="italic">contrahere, constringere</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer under <reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Isa 59:5</reference>); and that it can also be used of any kind of means of checking free movement, the Arab. 'ikâs, as the name of a cord with which the camel is made fast by the head and forefeet, shows. With this signification the interpretation is: <hi type="italic">et velut pedicâ</hi> (= וכבעכס) <hi type="italic">implicatus ad castigationem stulti</hi>, he follows her as if (bound) with a fetter to the punishment of the fool, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of himself (Michaelis, Fleischer, and others). Otherwise Luther, who first translated “in a fetter,” but afterwards (supplying ל, not ב): “and as if to fetters, where one corrects fools.” But the ellipsis is harsh, and the parallelism leads us to expect a living being in the place of עכס. Now since, according to Gesenius, עכס, fetter, can be equivalent to a fettered one neither at <reference osisRef="Isa.17.5">Isa 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">Isa 21:17</reference>, nor <reference osisRef="Prov.23.28">Pro 23:28</reference> (according to which עכס must at least have an active personal signification), we transpose the nouns of the clause and write וכאויל אל־מוּסר עכס, he follows her as a fool (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 292) to correction (restraint) with fetters; or if אויל is to be understood not so much physically as morally, and refers to self-destroying conduct (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Psa 107:7</reference>): as a madman, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a criminal, to chains. The one figure denotes the fate into which he rushes, like a beast devoid of reason, as the loss of life; and the other denotes the fate to which he permits himself to be led by that woman, like a criminal by the officer, as the loss of freedom and of honour.
entries.d5a42a44e59d0190a080906c25053dbdb781a761: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.24-Prov.7.25">Pro 7:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen10791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10792" type="x-p"/> With ועתּה, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.5.7">Pro 5:7</reference>, the author now brings his narrative to a close, adding the exhortation deduced from it: 24 And now, ye children, give ear unto me,      And observe the words of my mouth! 25 Let not thine heart incline to her ways,      And stray not in her paths. <div eID="gen10792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10793" type="x-p"/> The verb שׂטה (whence jēst, like jēt, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.15">Pro 4:15</reference>, with long ē from <hi type="italic">i</hi>) the author uses also of departure from a wicked way (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.15">Pro 4:15</reference>); but here, where the portraiture of a faithless wife (a סוטה) is presented, the word used in the law of jealousy, Num 5, for the trespass of an אשׁת אישׁ is specially appropriate. שׂטה is interchanged with תּעה (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.21.14">Gen 21:14</reference>): wander not on her paths, which would be the consequence of straying on them. Theodotion: καὶ μὴ πλανηθῇς ἐν ἀτραποῖς αὐτῆς, with καί, as also Syr., Targ., and Jerome. The Masora reckons this verse to the 25 which have אל at the beginning and ואל at the middle of each clause (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer in the <hi type="italic">Luth. Zeitschrift</hi>, 1865, p. 587); the text of Norzi has therefore correctly ואל, which is found also in good MSS (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the Erfurt, 2 and 3).
entries.6786fa9c99999161df35766d1e3c40755f87f399: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.26-Prov.7.27">Pro 7:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen10793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10794" type="x-p"/> The admonition, having its motive in that which goes before, is now founded on the emphatic finale: 26 For many are the slain whom she hath caused to fall,      And many are her slain. 27 A multiplicity of ways to help is her house,      Going down to the chambers of death. <div eID="gen10794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10795" type="x-p"/> The translation “for many slain has she laid low” (Syr., Targ., Jerome, Luther) is also syntactically possible; for רבּים can be placed before its substantive after the manner of the demonstratives and numerals (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.28">Neh 9:28</reference>, cf. אחד, Sol 4:9), and the accentuation which requires two servants (the usual two <hi type="italic">Munachs</hi>) to the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> appears indeed thus to construe it. It is otherwise if רבים here meant <hi type="italic">magni</hi> (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ralbag, and recently Bertheau), and not multi; but רבים and עצמים stand elsewhere in connection with each other in the signification many and numerous, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.18">Psa 35:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>; Mic 4:3. “Her slain” are those slain by her; the part. pass. is connected with the genitive of the actor, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference>; cf. (Arab.) ḳatyl âlmḥabbt, of one whom love kills (Fl.). With <reference osisRef="Prov.7.27">Pro 7:27</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference>; Pro 9:18. In 27a, בּיתהּ is not equivalent to בביתה after <reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">Pro 8:2</reference>, also not elliptical and equivalent to דרכי ביתה; the former is unnecessary, the latter is in no case established by <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>; Ezr 10:13, nor by <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>; 2Ki 23:17 (see, on the other hand, Philippi’s <hi type="italic">Status Constructus</hi>, pp. 87-93). Rightly Hitzig has: her house forms a multiplicity of ways to hell, in so far as adultery leads by a diversity of ways to hell. Similarly the subject and the predicate vary in number, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.25">Pro 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">Dan 9:23</reference>, and frequently. If one is once in her house, he may go in this or in that way, but surely his path is to destruction: it consists of many steps to hell, such as lead down (דרך, fem. <reference osisRef="Isa.37.34">Isa 37:34</reference>, masc. <reference osisRef="Isa.30.21">Isa 30:21</reference>) to the extreme depths of death (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference>, “chambers of the south” = its remotest regions veiling themselves in the invisible); for חדר (Arab. khiddr) is the part of the tent or the house removed farthest back, and the most private (Fl.). These חדרי־מות, cf. עמקי שׁאול, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference>, approach to the conception of גּיהנּם, which is afterwards distinguished from שאול.  <chapter eID="Prov.7"/> <div eID="gen10795" type="x-p"/>
